item.title: Housebuilding slump deepens as private construction falls 4.7%
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK’s housebuilding sector has faced a significant downturn, with private construction activity falling by 4.7% in the third quarter of 2026. This decline has contributed to a broader drop in construction output, raising concerns about the nation’s ability to meet housing demand. According to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), the overall construction output fell by 0.7% during the same period, marking a challenging quarter for the industry.

Housebuilding Challenges Intensify

The sharp decline in private housebuilding highlights the ongoing pressures facing developers. Rising borrowing costs and increasing construction expenses have made it more difficult for builders to maintain momentum. Whilst repair and maintenance activity saw a modest increase of 0.5%, it was not enough to offset the significant drop in new housing projects. Additionally, five out of nine construction sectors experienced declines, further underscoring the industry’s struggles.

September did bring a slight recovery, with construction output rising by 0.8% after four consecutive months of decline. New construction work increased by 0.9%, and repair and maintenance activity rose by 0.6%. Infrastructure projects provided the most significant boost, with output growing by 3.3% during the month. However, this monthly improvement was insufficient to reverse the overall quarterly decline, leaving the sector in a precarious position.

Rising Costs and Future Prospects

Despite the challenges, there were some positive signs for the future. Total new orders increased by 1.2% in the third quarter, equivalent to £107 million. This growth was primarily driven by public sector projects outside housing and private commercial construction. However, the rising cost of construction materials continues to pose a significant hurdle. Construction output prices increased by 3.2% in the 12 months to September 2026, adding to the financial pressures faced by developers and contractors.

Phil Hughes, deputy managing director of Paragon Bank SME Lending, commented on the situation: “September’s 0.8% rise in construction output offers some relief after four consecutive monthly falls, with growth across both new work and repair and maintenance. Infrastructure was the main contributor to the monthly increase in new work, which should support demand across the extensive network of SME contractors, equipment providers, and specialist firms.”

Whilst this uptick in infrastructure projects provides a glimmer of hope, the persistent decline in private housebuilding remains a critical issue. With the combination of weaker activity and rising costs, efforts to increase housing supply face significant challenges.

As the industry navigates these difficult conditions, homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to stay informed about how these trends could impact the housing market. Monitoring developments in construction activity and costs could provide valuable insights for those considering their next steps in the property landscape.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Chestertons and Knight Frank have announced key promotions within their London teams, signalling continued confidence in the capital’s prime property market. These strategic appointments come as estate agencies focus on strengthening their expertise in high-value residential sales and international investor relations.

Chestertons expands new homes leadership

Chestertons has promoted Ahmad Alazem to Central London Director for New Homes, reflecting the agency’s commitment to growing its new-build residential business across prime central locations. With five years at the firm and 14 years’ specialism in Middle Eastern investment markets, Alazem will oversee expansion across nine central London branches.

His remit includes developing relationships with property developers, attracting overseas buyers and improving inter-office collaboration. Alazem will continue leading Chestertons’ Middle East and North Africa desk – a role he’s held since mid-2024 – leveraging his extensive experience with international residential investments.

Alazem noted London’s enduring appeal for global investors, particularly from the Gulf region, stating: “With early signs of renewed market confidence, we’re well-positioned to enhance our luxury offerings and connect international buyers with central London opportunities.” Adam Jennings, Chestertons’ head of residential, highlighted Alazem’s “in-depth understanding of prime markets” as key to serving high-net-worth clients.

Knight Frank bolsters Marylebone team

In another senior appointment, Knight Frank has named Daniel Sugarman as head of sales for its Marylebone office – marking a return to where he began his property career in 2018. The promotion follows Sugarman’s recent stint leading core sales in Knightsbridge and his elevation to Partner in 2026.

With 13 years’ London market experience, Sugarman will oversee sales performance and regional partnerships for properties typically valued up to £4 million. His reappointment to Marylebone suggests Knight Frank’s focus on maintaining strong leadership in established prime central London markets, alongside its super-prime operations.

These strategic moves by leading agencies indicate continued confidence in London’s luxury property sector, particularly regarding international investment and premium new-build developments. For prospective buyers, such appointments may signal estate agents’ commitment to providing specialised expertise in competitive central London markets.

item.title: Mortgage arrears fall again – but industry warns worse may be ahead
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

UK mortgage arrears have declined for the tenth consecutive quarter, according to the latest industry figures, though experts caution that rising borrowing costs may create future challenges for homeowners and landlords. The data from UK Finance reveals homeowner arrears fell by 10% annually to 76,080 cases in the third quarter of 2026, while buy-to-let arreres dropped more sharply by 22% to 8,170.

However, the figures also show a quarterly rise in property repossessions, with 1,840 homeowner possessions recorded (a 3% increase from Q2) and 690 buy-to-let repossessions (up 10%). Despite these increases, repossession levels remain significantly lower than the previous year's figures.

Experts question whether arrears tell the full story

While the continued decline in mortgage arrears appears positive for the housing market, some industry professionals suggest these figures may conceal underlying financial pressures. Richard Pike of Phoebus Software noted that while falling arrears support market confidence, many households could be facing mounting challenges.

"Higher mortgage costs may take time to fully impact borrowers, particularly those who haven't yet refinanced onto current rates," Pike explained. He also highlighted concerns about rising unsecured borrowing, which might indicate some households are relying on credit to manage daily expenses.

The situation appears most acute for those facing both increased housing costs and changing personal circumstances, such as job changes or family situations. Industry observers suggest lenders are monitoring these trends closely and exploring support options for borrowers showing early signs of financial strain.

Affordability concerns persist across the market

NAEA Propertymark's Ian Harris welcomed the arrears reduction but emphasised that affordability remains a key challenge for both homeowners and property investors. Mortgage costs alongside general living expenses continue to affect buyer confidence and movement within the housing market, he noted.

The buy-to-let sector shows particular signs of pressure, with some suggesting that recent legislative changes, including the Renters' Rights Act, may be contributing to landlords' financial challenges. Mark Harris of SPF Private Clients pointed to the rise in minor arrears cases among landlords as a potential warning sign, though overall levels remain below previous years.

Looking ahead, industry figures stress the importance of maintaining a balanced property market where buyers, sellers and investors can operate with confidence. While current arrears figures offer encouragement, the combination of higher mortgage rates and wider economic factors suggests ongoing vigilance will be needed across the sector.

item.title: The unlikely town where room rents are rising faster than anywhere else
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Greater Manchester's Stockport has emerged as the UK's fastest-growing rental hotspot for room lettings, with prices rising at more than ten times the national average. New data reveals tenants in this commuter town now pay higher room rents than those in central Manchester, highlighting shifting dynamics in regional rental markets.

Stockport leads UK room rent rises

SpareRoom's latest figures show Stockport room rents surged 10.4% annually to reach £717 per month in Q3 2026 – £32 more than Manchester's £685 average. This dramatic increase compares to a modest 1% rise across UK room rents overall. The Greater Manchester town leads a group of 21 locations where room rents grew by at least 3%.

Other significant rent increases include:

  • Gloucester: +7.7% (£642 average)
  • Warrington: +7.4% (£625 average)
  • Belfast: +6.8% (£624 average)
  • Edgware: +6.6% (£861 average)

Supply crunch drives record prices

UK room rents hit a new peak of £769 per month as available properties fell 4.7% year-on-year. Seven of nine regions saw record highs, with particular pressure in the South West where Exeter recorded a 79.1% demand surge alongside its 4.5% rent increase to £681.

Market towns are experiencing extraordinary demand growth:

  • Chesham: 97.6% more enquiries (6.5 per room)
  • Kettering: 87% demand rise (6.8 enquiries per room)
  • Barnstaple: 82.1% increase (7 enquiries per room)

Bootle currently has the UK's most competitive room market, with 16 prospective tenants chasing each available property. The figures suggest renters are increasingly considering smaller towns and commuter locations, potentially driven by hybrid working patterns and central urban affordability issues.

Regional variations challenge renters

The data reveals stark differences between local markets. Whilst Stockport's rents accelerate, other areas like Preston (+4%) and Bolton (+3.1%) show more modest growth. Renters might consider these nearby alternatives where price rises remain below Stockport's dramatic surge.

With supply shrinking and demand patterns shifting unpredictably, tenants may wish to research local market conditions thoroughly. The widening gap between the fastest-growing locations and more stable markets could present opportunities for cost-conscious renters prepared to consider less competitive areas.

item.title: Section 21 ban fails to make most tenants feel more secure, research finds
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The abolition of Section 21 no-fault evictions, which came into effect in May 2026, has failed to significantly improve tenants’ feelings of security, according to recent research. Despite widespread support for the Renters’ Rights Act, fewer than four in ten tenants reported feeling more secure in their tenancies following the change. The findings highlight a gap between the expectations of tenants and the perceived impact of the legislation.

Mixed Reactions from Tenants

The Autumn 2026 Lettings Report by LRG revealed that whilst 68% of tenants supported the abolition of Section 21, only 39% felt more secure as a result. Nearly a third (31%) said their sense of security had not improved, and 13% even felt less secure. A further 17% were unsure or unaware of the reform altogether. These results raise questions about whether the legislation has achieved its intended goal of providing greater reassurance to tenants.

Landlords Question the Reform

The research also uncovered a significant divide between landlords and tenants regarding the abolition of Section 21. Just a third of landlords surveyed by LRG believed the change was necessary, with even lower support among LandlordZone respondents, where only one in five backed the reform. Interestingly, 65% of LRG landlords stated they had never used Section 21, while 24% had used it once, and 6% more than once. However, LandlordZone landlords reported higher usage, with 59% having used Section 21 at least once.

Relationships Over Legal Protections

Despite differing views on the legislation, both landlords and tenants placed significant importance on relationships when assessing tenancy security. Among tenants, 27% identified a good relationship with their landlord as the most important factor, while 25% highlighted effective communication and management by letting agents. Only 20% of tenants cited legal protections as their primary concern. Landlords placed even greater emphasis on relationships, with 44% of LRG landlords and 65% of LandlordZone landlords viewing a positive landlord-tenant relationship as crucial for security. In contrast, just 7% of LRG landlords and 3% of LandlordZone landlords prioritised legal protections.

The findings suggest that whilst legislative changes like the abolition of Section 21 aim to improve tenant security, day-to-day management and communication remain key factors in fostering trust and stability in the rental market.

item.title: First-time buyers retreat as mortgage rate rise triggers sharp drop in demand
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market is experiencing a notable slowdown, with first-time buyer enquiries dropping by 27% compared to last year, according to recent data from Zoopla. This decline comes amidst rising mortgage rates, which have reduced buyers’ purchasing power by an estimated 15% since the start of 2023. The Bank of England’s decision to increase the base rate to 4% has further exacerbated affordability challenges, prompting many prospective homeowners to delay their property plans.

Southern markets face mounting pressure

The impact of higher borrowing costs is particularly evident in southern England, where the housing market is showing clear signs of strain. In the South East, property listings have surged by 12.4% year-on-year, whilst sales agreed have fallen by 16.2%. Similarly, the East of England has seen a 17% increase in available homes alongside a 7.6% drop in sales. London has not been immune to this trend, with a 6% rise in available stock and a 6.1% decline in sales agreed. Average house prices in these regions have also softened, with declines ranging from 0.4% to 1% annually.

This growing mismatch between supply and demand is putting significant pressure on sellers to adjust their asking prices. The South West, for instance, has recorded a 12% increase in available properties, while prices have fallen by 0.4%. These figures suggest that affordability constraints, driven by higher mortgage rates, are reshaping market dynamics in the south.

North-south divide persists

In contrast to southern regions, northern England continues to see annual house price growth, despite weaker sales activity. The North West and North East have recorded price increases of 3.2% and 2.4% respectively. However, sales agreed have fallen sharply, dropping by 16.4% in the North West and 23.5% in the North East. This highlights that even in more affordable markets, higher borrowing costs are affecting transaction volumes.

Scotland stands out as the only region to buck the trend, with a 1.4% increase in sales agreed and a 2.5% rise in house prices. This resilience may reflect the region’s relatively lower property prices and differing market conditions.

More options for first-time buyers

Despite the broader slowdown in demand, first-time buyers who are able to secure mortgage finance may find more opportunities in the current market. Zoopla’s data reveals a 14% annual increase in the availability of two-bedroom houses, a popular choice among first-time purchasers. Additionally, the number of properties priced below £200,000 has risen by 13%, offering greater choice at the more affordable end of the market.

Richard Donnell, executive director at Zoopla, commented: “First-time buyers remain a vital part of the housing market, accounting for four in ten sales last year. While higher mortgage rates have impacted affordability, those who can secure financing now have access to a wider range of properties.”

As the market continues to adjust to higher borrowing costs, homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to carefully evaluate their options. With supply increasing and prices softening in many areas, opportunities may emerge for those well-positioned to navigate the current climate.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #462
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent developments in the private rented sector highlight significant shifts in landlord management strategies, compliance challenges, and potential data sharing between government bodies. With regulatory pressures mounting, property investors face important decisions about how to operate their portfolios efficiently whilst meeting legal obligations.

Landlords Adapt Management Approaches Amid Compliance Demands

New research reveals that 65% of landlords have altered their property management structures over the past two years. The findings from property management platform August show polarising trends, with 27% of landlords moving away from letting agents whilst 26% have actually begun using them. Cost considerations and desire for greater control appear key drivers, with 22% seeking more hands-on management and 14% switching due to letting fees.

For those employing agents, the survey indicates substantial variations in fees, with 58% paying 11% or more of rental income and one in ten landlords facing charges exceeding 15%. Industry experts suggest compliance burdens are creating a bifurcated market, where some investors turn to professional agents whilst others adopt digital tools to manage properties directly.

PRS Database May Expand Information Sharing

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook has confirmed the government hasn't ruled out sharing Private Rented Sector database information with other authorities, including HMRC and local councils. Any data sharing would need to comply with data protection laws and maintain proportionality, with specific arrangements to be formalised in future legislation after the initial database rollout.

This potential expansion of data access aims to support statutory functions across government bodies, though exact parameters remain under discussion. Landlords may wish to ensure their property records remain accurate in anticipation of these possible changes.

Clarification on Empty Property Rules

Contrary to some media reports, councils cannot automatically seize properties vacant for six months. New rules reducing the qualifying period from two years still require local authorities to apply to the First Tier Tribunal (Property Chamber) and demonstrate:

  • Conclusive evidence of six months' vacancy
  • No immediate prospect of occupation
  • Reasonable attempts to contact the owner
  • Clear intentions for the property's use

Industry body Propertymark stresses that reaching the six-month threshold doesn't trigger automatic action, with tribunal scrutiny maintaining important safeguards for property owners.

As the regulatory landscape evolves, landlords face increasingly complex decisions about management strategies, compliance costs and operational transparency. Staying informed about these developments could help property investors navigate the changing private rented sector effectively.

item.title: The UK property market is apparently at death’s door
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent headlines painting a bleak picture of the UK property market might not tell the full story. Whilst some estate agents report challenges, the latest data reveals a more nuanced situation with steady buyer activity continuing across many regions.

Market Activity Defies Negative Narratives

Property listings and sales figures suggest the market remains active despite economic uncertainties. Week 44 saw 28,700 new listings enter the market - slightly higher than the previous week's 27,500 and marginally above the 10-year average for this period. Year-to-date figures show:

  • 1.557 million new listings in 2026 (0.1% below 2025)
  • 8.8% higher than both 2023 and the 2017-19 average
  • 7.8% above the last decade's average

Sales agreed figures tell a similar story, with 20,500 properties going under offer in week 44. Whilst this represents a seasonal dip of 5.9% from the previous week, this follows the typical decade-average pattern for autumn.

Behind the Headlines: Estate Agency Practices Under Scrutiny

Some industry analysts suggest that certain estate agency strategies may contribute to perceptions of a struggling market. Common issues reportedly include:

  • Overvaluing properties to secure instructions
  • Delaying necessary price adjustments
  • Blaming market conditions when sales stall

Net sales figures (accounting for failed transactions) stand at 14,900 for week 44, bringing the year-to-date total to 1.053 million completed sales. This represents:

  • A 10.3% increase from 2023 levels
  • 4% above pre-pandemic 2017-19 averages
  • Just 2% below the decade average

For homeowners considering selling, these figures suggest the market remains functional, though perhaps requiring more realistic pricing strategies than during the post-pandemic boom years. Those monitoring local markets might find regional variations more significant than national headlines suggest.

As always, working with reputable agents who provide evidence-based valuations and transparent communication appears crucial in the current climate. The data indicates that whilst the market has cooled from its peak, reports of its demise appear greatly exaggerated.

item.title: Leasehold reforms under fire as lawyers warn flat owners may not save a penny
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Millions of leaseholders in England are set to gain enhanced rights to challenge service charges under new government reforms, but property lawyers have raised concerns over whether these changes will translate into tangible savings. From April 2027, flat owners will have stronger protections against opaque billing practices and landlords’ legal costs during disputes. Additional measures, effective from November 2027, will introduce stricter regulations on insurance fees, financial reporting and billing transparency. While the reforms aim to alleviate financial pressures on leaseholders, experts caution that they may not address the root causes of rising costs.

Will Reforms Actually Reduce Costs?

Housing minister Matthew Pennycook has emphasised that the reforms aim to improve fairness and transparency in service charges, enabling leaseholders to more effectively challenge unreasonable increases. However, industry professionals remain sceptical. Jo Ironside, partner at Mayo Wynne Baxter, noted that whilst transparency is welcome, it does not tackle the underlying drivers of escalating service charges. She highlighted rising insurance premiums, contractor fees and building safety obligations as key factors contributing to higher costs. Ironside also cautioned that replacing leasehold with commonhold, often touted as a solution, would not eliminate these expenses. Instead, it could burden residents with complex decisions regarding maintenance, insurance and building management.

Challenges for Landlords and Managing Agents

The reforms also introduce stricter requirements for landlords and managing agents, who will need to adapt to new regulations. Mark Chick, partner at Bishop & Sewell and director of the Association of Leasehold Enfranchisement Practitioners (ALEP), welcomed the changes but highlighted the significant responsibilities they impose. Managing agents, in particular, will face tougher obligations, including enhanced financial reporting and greater accountability in billing practices. Jonathan Turner, partner and head of residential conveyancing at Morr & Co, described the reforms as gradual but necessary, urging landlords, leaseholders and their advisers to stay informed about the evolving landscape.

Whilst the government’s leasehold reforms aim to empower leaseholders and improve transparency, their ability to reduce costs remains uncertain. Rising operational expenses and building safety requirements continue to drive service charges higher, and greater transparency alone may not suffice. Leaseholders, landlords and managing agents alike will need to navigate these changes carefully, ensuring compliance whilst balancing financial pressures.

item.title: Landlord possession claims surge as court backlog fears grow
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The final countdown to England's Section 21 reforms saw an unprecedented surge in landlord possession claims, with accelerated cases nearly doubling in recent months. Ministry of Justice data reveals a 68% annual increase in accelerated possession claims during the third quarter of 2026, reaching a record 12,156 cases between July and September.

Deadline rush creates court pressure

Landlords raced to secure possession orders before the 31 July deadline for existing Section 21 notices, following the abolition of no-fault evictions on 1 May 2026. The quarterly figures show accelerated claims accounted for 43% of all 28,249 landlord possession claims, representing over 95% of the total recorded throughout 2025. Despite this influx, completed repossessions actually fell by 10% year-on-year to 6,886, suggesting growing processing delays.

Eviction specialist Landlord Action reported one of its busiest months on record in July, with instructions nearly halving in August before recovering 30% in September. Paul Shamplina, the firm's founder, noted: "The figures demonstrate how landlords urgently finalised existing Section 21 cases before the legislative changes took full effect. Many brought forward possession action as a precaution against the new rules."

Landlord exits could shrink rental supply

Industry observers highlight concerning trends behind the statistics, with approximately 30% of possession cases reportedly involving landlords planning to sell properties. Shamplina warned: "This significant proportion suggests more tenants may face relocation challenges when suitable rental accommodation is already scarce."

The changing landscape comes alongside several financial pressures for landlords, including:

  • Higher property income tax rates effective from April 2027
  • Increased regulatory requirements under the Renters' Rights Act
  • Growing operational costs across the private rental sector

Landlord Action also noted shifting approaches to rent arrears, with some property owners taking swifter action than previously observed. The combination of financial pressures and regulatory changes continues to reshape landlord strategies across England's private rental market.

As the sector adapts to post-Section 21 regulations, both landlords and tenants may wish to stay informed about evolving possession processes and housing rights. The full impact of these changes on rental supply and pricing will likely become clearer in coming quarters.

item.title: Seven in ten landlords consider rent hikes as property tax rise looms
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A significant number of landlords in the UK are contemplating rent increases ahead of impending tax changes, according to recent research. The findings, commissioned by LegalforLandlords, reveal that 70% of landlords are considering raising rents in response to a four-percentage-point increase in property income tax rates set to take effect from April 2027. This shift has sparked concerns about the potential impact on rental affordability and housing supply across the private rented sector.

Rent Increases on the Horizon

The survey highlights that 32% of landlords plan to raise rents specifically to offset the additional tax burden, while a further 38% are considering similar measures. Only 22% indicated they would absorb the extra costs, and 8% felt their local rental markets could not sustain further increases. These intentions suggest that tenants may face higher rental costs in the coming years, particularly as landlords grapple with rising operational expenses and taxation pressures.

Potential Reduction in Property Portfolios

In addition to rent adjustments, nearly half (47%) of landlords are exploring ways to reduce their property investments. This includes 23% who are considering selling one or more rental properties and 17% who may sell their entire portfolios. More broadly, 61% of respondents are either actively planning to exit the private rented sector or seriously contemplating doing so. Such trends could lead to a decline in rental property availability, further tightening the market and limiting tenant options.

Impact on Investment Plans and Profitability

The tax changes are also influencing landlords’ investment decisions, with 45% stating they have decided against purchasing additional properties. Only 2% of those surveyed expressed intentions to expand their portfolios, while 35% had no plans to invest further regardless of the tax adjustments. Moreover, nearly three-quarters of landlords expect their profits to be affected, with 37% anticipating a substantial reduction and another 37% predicting a noticeable decline. Just 6% believe their profitability will remain unaffected.

These findings underscore the broader challenges facing the private rented sector, as landlords navigate higher costs and regulatory changes. With many expressing dissatisfaction with the tax adjustments, the long-term implications for both landlords and tenants remain a topic of concern. As the sector evolves, homeowners may wish to carefully assess their financial strategies to adapt to these shifting dynamics.

item.title: Estate agents brace for further sales slump as housing outlook hits three-year low
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK housing market is facing growing challenges, with estate agents anticipating a further slowdown in property sales. According to the latest Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) Residential Market Survey, sales expectations have fallen to their lowest level since July 2023, reflecting a three-year low in market confidence. Factors such as elevated mortgage rates and economic uncertainty are contributing to a subdued outlook, with buyer demand remaining weak and house prices under renewed pressure.

Sales Expectations Hit a Low

The RICS survey reveals a net balance of -17% for sales expectations over the next 12 months, marking the weakest reading in over three years. Short-term forecasts are similarly pessimistic, with a net balance of -11% predicting weaker sales in the next three months. This decline follows a trend of deteriorating market conditions, with agreed sales also worsening. The net balance for agreed sales fell to -24% in October, down from -18% in September, representing the lowest figure in three months.

New buyer enquiries remained stagnant, with a net balance of -24% in October, unchanged from September. Nearly all regions across the UK reported either declining or flat demand, indicating a lack of momentum in the market. Additionally, fewer homeowners are listing their properties for sale, with new instructions dropping to a net balance of -8%. This reversal from September’s positive reading of +6% suggests a potential reduction in new listings in the coming months.

House Prices Face Downward Pressure

House prices are also experiencing renewed downward pressure, with the headline price balance slipping to -36% in October, down from -34% in September. This marks the second consecutive monthly decline, following a period of relative stability during the summer. Regions such as London, the South East, East Anglia, and the West Midlands are particularly affected, reporting weak price trends. However, the picture remains mixed across the UK, with Northern Ireland continuing to see firm price growth and Scotland and the North West of England recording modest increases.

Expectations for house prices over the next 12 months have weakened sharply, with the balance falling from zero to -17%. Despite this, respondents’ forecasts suggest a relatively modest decline of around 1%, indicating that while prices may soften, significant drops are not anticipated.

Rental Market Tightens Further

While the sales market struggles, the private rental sector continues to face tightening conditions. Tenant demand has returned to modest growth, with the quarterly net balance rising to +7% from -1%. However, landlord instructions remain firmly negative, exacerbating the supply-demand imbalance. This trend is likely to place further upward pressure on rental prices, adding to the challenges faced by tenants.

The RICS survey highlights a challenging period for the UK housing market, with weak buyer demand, declining sales, and softening house prices. Whilst regional variations persist, the overall outlook suggests a cautious approach for both buyers and sellers. For those considering entering the market, staying informed about local trends and seeking professional advice could be beneficial in navigating these uncertain conditions.

item.title: Buy-to-let warning sign as new property company formations plunge 25%
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The number of new property companies formed in the UK has seen a notable decline, dropping by over a quarter in October compared to the same period last year. Recent data highlights a significant shift in activity, with property company formations falling by 25.4% year-on-year, from 8,070 to 6,020. This trend, which began earlier in the year, suggests a broader slowdown in the buy-to-let market, raising concerns about its impact on the private rented sector.

What’s Behind the Decline?

The drop in property company formations marks a sharp reversal from earlier in the year, when numbers were on the rise. During the first three months of 2026, formations increased by 1%, but the third quarter saw a decline of 22.8%. Overall, the data reveals a 14.3% decrease in formations between January and October compared to the same period in 2025, with 10,691 fewer companies established. If this trend continues, 2026 could become the first year since records began in 2016 to see an annual decline, ending nine consecutive years of growth.

One potential factor behind this slowdown is the increasing financial pressures facing landlords. Limited company structures have become a popular choice for buy-to-let investors, particularly for tax efficiency and portfolio management. However, the latest figures suggest that fewer investors are opting to set up new corporate entities, perhaps due to higher mortgage rates, regulatory changes, or economic uncertainty.

Implications for the Rental Market

The decline in property company formations could have wider implications for the private rented sector. With fewer investors entering the market, there may be a reduction in the supply of rental properties, particularly in areas where demand already outstrips availability. This could place further pressure on rental prices, making it more challenging for tenants to find affordable housing.

For landlords, the slowdown may limit opportunities to expand their portfolios, particularly in competitive markets. Letting agents and tenants alike could face challenges as the supply of rental homes tightens. Whilst the figures alone do not provide a complete picture, they highlight the need for careful consideration of the factors influencing the buy-to-let market.

Looking Ahead

The current trend raises questions about the future of buy-to-let investment in the UK. Investors may wish to weigh the potential benefits of limited company structures against the broader economic and regulatory landscape. As the market continues to evolve, staying informed about changes in mortgage rates, tax policies, and rental demand could help landlords make well-informed decisions.

Whilst the decline in property company formations is significant, it remains to be seen whether this trend will persist in the long term. For now, homeowners and investors alike may wish to monitor market developments closely to understand the potential impact on their portfolios and the wider rental sector.

item.title: First-time buyers borrow more as mortgage rates hit three-year high
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

First-time buyers are increasingly stretching their finances to secure homes, as mortgage rates reach their highest levels in three years. Recent data highlights a growing trend towards higher loan-to-value (LTV) mortgages, with lenders expanding options for those with smaller deposits. However, rising borrowing costs continue to present significant challenges for aspiring homeowners.

Higher LTV mortgages gain traction

The mortgage market has seen a notable shift towards products catering to buyers with limited deposits. In October, the number of 95% LTV mortgage deals increased from 468 to 474, while 90% LTV products now represent around 24% of mainstream mortgage options. This expansion comes as lenders adapt to growing demand from first-time buyers struggling to save substantial deposits.

However, borrowers with larger deposits have seen their choices diminish. The selection of 60% LTV mortgages fell from 753 to 706 products – the lowest availability since March 2024. This contraction has pushed the average LTV across mainstream mortgages to a record 79.31%, the highest level since electronic records began in 2011.

Affordability pressures intensify

Despite greater product availability, higher borrowing costs remain a hurdle. The Moneyfacts Average New Mortgage Rate reached 5.89% in early November, up from 5.83% in October. Two-year fixed rates now average 5.97%, with five-year deals at 6%. For 95% LTV mortgages, rates are even steeper at 6.37% for two-year fixes and 6.33% for five-year terms.

ONS data reveals first-time buyers are borrowing more relative to both property values and incomes. The median LTV for this group hit 85.6% in 2025 – the highest level since before the 2008 financial crisis. Meanwhile, the average house-price-to-income ratio has climbed from 3.7 in 2006 to 4.3 in 2025. UK Finance figures also show the typical first-time buyer age has risen from 31 to 33 over the past decade.

Moneyfacts finance expert Rachel Springall notes: "Affordability constraints are pushing first-time buyers towards higher LTV options or larger loan-to-income ratios, often exceeding five times their salary, as they attempt to stretch their budgets."

With mortgage rates at three-year highs and property prices remaining elevated, first-time buyers face difficult choices between delaying their purchase, compromising on location or property type, or taking on greater financial commitments. Those considering entering the market might benefit from exploring all available mortgage options and seeking independent financial advice.

item.title: Prime London sales slump as price cuts mount and rents rise 5%
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

London's prime property market continues to face headwinds, with new data revealing significant price adjustments and falling sales volumes. Meanwhile, the capital's rental market shows robust growth as supply tightens, creating markedly different conditions for buyers and tenants.

Prime sales market sees price corrections

October proved challenging for prime London sales, with transactions down 17.5% year-on-year according to LonRes data. This represents the weakest October performance since 2018, with activity also sitting 6.6% below pre-pandemic averages. The slowdown comes as buyers demonstrate increased price sensitivity in the current economic climate.

Around half of all listed properties have undergone at least one price reduction, with accepted offers averaging 10.3% below initial asking prices. Compared to peak 2021/22 levels, prime London values have fallen 11.9%, with prime central London experiencing a steeper 15.8% decline. The figures suggest homeowners may need to adjust expectations to secure sales in the current market.

Super-prime segment shows resilience

The £5m-plus market displayed some resilience amidst the wider slowdown, with October transactions rising 13.6% annually. However, the longer-term picture remains subdued, with year-to-date super-prime sales down 6.8% compared to 2022. Market analysts suggest political and fiscal uncertainty may be contributing to caution among high-net-worth buyers.

New sales instructions across all price brackets fell 7.2%, while properties going under offer dropped more sharply at 21.3%. These indicators suggest the current slowdown may persist into 2024 without significant economic improvements or policy changes to boost buyer confidence.

Rental market strengthens as supply dwindles

In contrast to the sales market, prime London lettings recorded 5% annual rental growth in October - the strongest increase since early 2025. Rents now stand 44% above pre-pandemic levels, creating challenging conditions for tenants.

The rental supply crunch continues to intensify, with new instructions down 14.9% year-on-year and total available properties 2% lower. Despite this, agreed lets increased 3.5%, demonstrating sustained demand from tenants who may be postponing purchase plans amid economic uncertainty.

This divergence between sales and lettings markets presents different considerations for property investors and homeowners. While vendors face price sensitivity and longer marketing periods, landlords benefit from strong tenant demand and rising yields - though regulatory changes may affect this balance in future.

item.title: Mortgage Advice Bureau drops full name in major rebrand
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

One of the UK's largest mortgage advisory networks has unveiled a significant rebrand, shortening its name from Mortgage Advice Bureau to Mab as part of a strategic shift towards broader homeownership support. The change reflects the company's ambition to engage with customers at every stage of their property journey, rather than focusing solely on mortgage advice.

A new identity for expanded services

Founded in 2000, the business has grown to become a major player in the mortgage market with over 2,100 advisers nationwide. The simplified Mab branding went live across digital platforms and customer communications this week, with appointed representative firms gradually adopting the new identity over coming months.

The rebrand comes as homeowners increasingly turn to digital tools and AI-powered solutions for initial property research. Mab aims to position itself as a long-term partner for property buyers, offering support that begins before mortgage applications and continues well beyond completion.

Supporting the entire homeownership journey

Peter Brodnicki, Mab's founder and CEO, explained the rationale behind the change: "Our original name perfectly described our mortgage-focused offering in 2000, but today's business supports customers through much more than just securing a home loan. As consumer behaviours evolve with digital innovation, we're adapting to meet these changing needs."

The company plans to leverage technology to streamline administrative processes, freeing up advisers to dedicate more time to customer relationships. This aligns with Mab's stated ambition to "power UK homeownership" by guiding clients through each stage of their property journey, from initial research to long-term financial planning.

  • Maintains existing FCA authorisation and protections
  • No changes to customer accounts or services
  • Parent company stock ticker remains unchanged
  • Advisers continue operating under current regulatory permissions

Brodnicki emphasised that while the outward identity is changing, the company's core values and commitment to customers remain unchanged. The rebrand represents an evolution rather than a fundamental shift in business operations, with existing clients unaffected by the transition.

As the mortgage market continues to evolve with technological advancements, this rebrand positions Mab to support homeowners through an increasingly digital property landscape while maintaining the personal advice that has built its reputation over 26 years.

item.title: Tax rise prompts price increases and exits
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent changes to rental income tax rules are prompting significant shifts in the UK property market, with many landlords considering rent increases or even exiting the sector altogether. According to a survey by Pegasus Insight, 73% of landlords are planning to raise rents, whilst 52% are contemplating selling their rental properties. These decisions come as the new tax measures begin to impact landlords’ profitability.

Understanding the Tax Changes

The changes to rental income tax rules mean landlords can no longer deduct mortgage interest from their rental income before calculating their tax liability. Instead, they receive a tax credit based on 20% of their mortgage interest payments. This shift has reduced the profitability of buy-to-let investments for many landlords, particularly those in higher tax brackets. As a result, landlords are exploring ways to offset these additional costs.

Potential Impact on Tenants and the Market

With a majority of landlords planning rent increases, tenants may face higher housing costs in the near future. This could exacerbate the affordability crisis in the rental market, particularly in areas where demand already outstrips supply. Additionally, the potential exodus of landlords selling their properties could lead to a rise in available housing stock, which might ease pressure on the sales market. However, this could also reduce the number of rental properties available, further driving up rents for those who rely on the private rental sector.

Options for Landlords

Landlords affected by the tax changes may wish to consider their options carefully. Some are exploring the possibility of incorporating their property portfolios into limited companies, where mortgage interest payments can still be deducted as a business expense. However, this route comes with its own complexities and costs, including stamp duty and capital gains tax implications. Others are reviewing their portfolios to identify underperforming properties that could be sold to reduce their tax burden.

As the property market adjusts to these tax changes, both landlords and tenants will need to stay informed about how they might be affected. Seeking professional advice could help landlords navigate the new landscape and make decisions that align with their financial goals.

item.title: Newcastle offers highest rental yield for investors
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research has identified Newcastle as the UK city offering the highest rental yields for property investors, with returns reaching up to 6.9% in some areas. The findings come as landlords across the country navigate changing tax landscapes and evolving rental market conditions.

Regional variations in rental yields

Recent analysis by Rushbrook Research highlights significant regional disparities in rental yields across Britain. While Newcastle leads the market with yields between 5.2% and 6.9%, other northern cities including Liverpool and Manchester also show strong performance, delivering average yields above 5%.

In contrast, southern cities tend to offer lower percentage returns despite higher property values. London properties showed some of the lowest yields at 2.9-4.1%, reflecting the capital's premium house prices relative to rental income potential. The research suggests investors might achieve better cash flow from properties in northern cities, though capital growth prospects vary across regions.

Tax considerations for landlords

The research emerges as buy-to-let investors face increased property income tax burdens following recent legislative changes. Since the phased reduction of mortgage interest tax relief completed in 2020, landlords now receive a 20% tax credit rather than deducting interest from their rental income.

Property investors might wish to consider:

  • Incorporating their portfolio to potentially benefit from corporation tax rates
  • Reviewing rental pricing strategies to maintain yields after tax
  • Exploring areas with strong rental demand relative to property prices

While higher-yielding areas like Newcastle present attractive income potential, prospective investors should carefully assess all costs including mortgage rates, maintenance expenses and void periods. Professional financial advice could help determine the most suitable investment strategy based on individual circumstances and long-term objectives.

item.title: Tenants spent more of income on rent in October
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New figures from HomeLet show that UK tenants are now dedicating a larger proportion of their incomes to rent, despite a slight dip in average monthly rental costs. The data reveals renters spent 32.7% of their earnings on housing in October, highlighting ongoing affordability pressures in the private rental sector.

Rental affordability worsens despite price dip

October saw average rents across the UK fall by 0.9% compared to previous months, marking a rare decrease in the typically upward-trending rental market. However, this modest price reduction hasn't translated into improved affordability for tenants. The proportion of income spent on rent actually increased, suggesting that earnings haven't kept pace with housing costs over the longer term.

Regional variations show London remains the most challenging area for renters, where housing costs consume a significantly higher percentage of take-home pay compared to other parts of the country. Meanwhile, some northern regions continue to offer relatively more affordable rental options, though affordability pressures are becoming more widespread nationwide.

What this means for renters and homeowners

For tenants, these figures underscore the importance of budgeting carefully for housing costs. Many renters might consider reviewing their current living arrangements to explore more affordable alternatives, particularly if they're spending above the recommended 30% of income on rent.

Prospective first-time buyers could view these affordability challenges as motivation to explore homeownership options. With rental costs consuming such a significant portion of incomes, some may find that mortgage payments could offer better long-term value, depending on individual circumstances and local property prices.

Landlords and property investors may need to take note of these affordability pressures when setting rents. While market conditions currently favour landlords in many areas, sustained affordability issues could eventually impact tenant demand and rent payment reliability.

As the cost-of-living squeeze continues, both renters and homeowners may wish to review their housing finances carefully. While the rental market shows some signs of fluctuation, the broader trend suggests housing costs remain a significant burden for many households across the UK.

item.title: Timing may matter more than rate rise for landlords
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

With interest rates continuing to climb, buy-to-let landlords face growing financial pressures when refinancing their mortgages. New analysis suggests that whilst rate rises are concerning, the timing of remortgaging could prove even more crucial for property investors managing cash flow.

Refinancing challenges for landlords

As fixed-rate mortgage deals expire, many landlords are facing significantly higher borrowing costs compared to when they initially secured their loans. Industry experts highlight that those coming off two or five-year fixed rates may see their monthly repayments increase by hundreds of pounds, creating immediate cash flow pressures.

The situation is particularly challenging for portfolio landlords with multiple properties, where simultaneous rate rises across several mortgages could substantially impact profitability. Some investors might need to consider restructuring their portfolios or exploring different financing strategies to maintain viable rental businesses.

Why timing matters

Mortgage specialists emphasise that proactive planning could help mitigate some financial strain. Landlords approaching the end of their current deal may wish to:

  • Begin researching remortgage options 4-6 months before their fixed rate expires
  • Compare products across the whole market, not just their existing lender
  • Consider professional advice to navigate complex portfolio financing
  • Assess whether product transfer deals offer better value than remortgaging

Those with mortgages maturing in the coming months might find that acting early could secure more favourable terms before potential further rate increases. However, borrowers should be aware that early repayment charges may apply if switching before their current deal ends.

For landlords concerned about affordability, it could be worth reviewing rental yields and property values, as some may need to adjust rents or reconsider their investment strategy. The current climate underlines the importance of stress testing finances against higher interest rate scenarios.

While market conditions remain challenging, careful planning and professional advice may help landlords navigate this period of rising costs. Keeping abreast of mortgage market developments and acting at the optimal time could make a material difference to long-term investment returns.
